subject: English Literature

subject: English Literature
content: Comparison of poems dealing with ideas about first-hand experience of conflict on the individual, such as ‘Bayonet Charge’, or ‘Remains’. Possible comparison between individual and collective experience of conflict, such as ‘War Photographer’, or ‘Charge of the Light Brigade’, or ‘Kamikaze’. Possible consideration of wider types of conflict, such as the impact of power dynamics in ‘London’, or in ‘Checking Out Me History’. Valid comparison of different ideas about conflict, such as ‘War Photographer’, or ‘Poppies’. Possible consideration of conflict with nature/the elements such as ‘Storm on the Island’. Valid comparison of the ways places have the potential to affect people’s lives in different ways, such as the urban environment in ‘A Wider View’, or ‘Homing’, or the natural environment in ‘Shall earth no more inspire thee’ or ‘Lines Written in Early Spring’, or ‘With Birds You’re Never Lonely’. Possible comparative treatment of how attitudes towards places can affect people’s lives, such as ‘A Portable Paradise’, or ‘With Birds You’re Never Lonely’. Any valid treatment of different interpretations of ‘place’, such as memories of previously-known places in ‘Name Journeys’ or ‘With Birds You’re Never Lonely’ or ‘A Portable Paradise’, or socially-constructed places such as societal structures and how these affect people’s lives, such as ‘England in 1819’ or ‘A Century Later’ or ‘Thirteen’. Any comparison of positive and negative effects of living in different places on people’s lives, such as ‘Pot’ or ‘Name Journeys’, or ‘On an Afternoon Train’. Ideas about family, memories, relationships and their effects on people. Ideas about the possible pressures of family and past experiences. Any valid treatment of wider ideas about the importance of home, family, or of memories. Ideas about the permanent effects of home and family. Possible treatment of the mixture of good and bad in terms of life experiences and how they shape and define us.

subject: English Literature
content: Use and effect of particular features to create meanings, such as effects of sibilance, or repetition, or imagery. Relevant treatment of the use of natural imagery to present ideas about conflict, such as ‘Storm on the Island’, or ‘Bayonet Charge’. Possible contrast in perspective between, for example, ‘War Photographer’, or ‘Poppies’. The use and effects of imagery to present ideas about urban/industrialised landscapes, such as ‘A Wider View’ or ‘Homing’. Possible contrast of the ways more natural types of places are presented, such as ‘A Portable Paradise’, or ‘Lines Written in Early Spring’. Different types of voice/perspective, such as nature’s voice in ‘Shall earth no more inspire thee’, or the presentation of the effects of time in ‘A Portable Paradise’. Possible comparison of the more formal mode of presentation with more anecdotal, lyrical forms such as ‘On an Afternoon Train’ or ‘Thirteen’. Possible comparison between use of language to present ideas, such as prosaic language in ‘Homing’, or more lyrical language in ‘Lines Written in Early Spring’. Possible use/effects of structure to present important ideas, such as stanza forms in ‘Shall earth no more inspire thee’, or narrative structure in ‘On an Afternoon Train’. Possible effects of use of positive and/or negative language to present ideas about home/family: ‘burn/dent/stain/grief/burned’, ‘laughter/candles’. Valid treatment of symbolism of ‘table’ as representative for family/memories/past. Possible examination of particular word choices to present ideas, such as suggestion of permanent effects of family suggested by ‘burn/dent/stain’. Comments related to effects of repeated phrases/grammatical features such as repeated pattern of ‘too much/too many’. Possible examination of effects of structural elements, such as use and effects of first and last line. Examination of use/effect of plural personal pronoun. Use of symbolism to present wider ideas about the significance of home/family. Possible contrast between use of plural/singular person to present ideas. Possible comparison/contrast between tone, such as more nuanced feelings in ‘Table’ compared with unambiguous tone of ‘Like a Beacon’. Use of symbolism in both poems, such as furniture/food. Any valid treatment of connection between use of particular aspect of home as representative of wider ideas, such as food as nurture/connection. Valid connection/contrast between use of titles to present ideas about connection, such as ‘table’ and ‘beacon’.

subject: English Literature
content: Ideas about the influence of parents on childhood. Ideas about identity and how this changes with growing up. Ideas about changing attitudes towards parents over time. Possible treatment of childhood perspective and how this might change with growing up. Any valid ideas about responsibility towards others. Ideas about patriotism/duty. Ideas about power/powerlessness. Possible exploration of ideas about the ways individuals are affected by wider conflict. Ideas about conflict with the natural world. Possible consideration of ideas about the impact of the powerful on society. Ideas about the impact that places can have on people’s lives and attitudes. Possible exploration of the negative impact of places on people’s lives, or sense of self, or attitudes towards others. Any valid exploration of ideas about society and its effects on individuals/groups. Any valid treatment of different types of ‘places’, such as mental/emotional places, or memories, or place in society, as well as day-to-day living places. Ideas about the effects of rural/urban landscape on people’s lives.
